title: From Architect to Online Personal Trainer: Quitting a Career to Coach
paragraphs: Callum: The the biggest thing that I've had, and this all wrote me back around to what I invited you on for in the first place, is you were actually one of the first creators. So I started working in fitness around COVID, and during that time I found your page on Instagram, and every morning was you either walking to work or walking to the gym. With your, you know, your morning debrief, what you're gonna do with the day, how to set yourself up for the day. And I think the main question is that I wanted to ask was the journey point. So that's where you really started, was it?

I know you've been doing it for around 8 years, but you started being really more proactive online around the COVID time. That start point for you, and given your little bit of history that I've looked up About, you know, your times of maybe bullying and self-consciousness and confidence and everything like that. How do you now see yourself? Because you are a leader by absolutely no title whatsoever. You've established yourself a leader because you're helping people change their lives. How does somebody go from those experiences when they're younger to be a leader of people? Josh: Oh mate, thank you for calling me a leader of people. That, that means a lot. Thank you so much. Um, repetition.

Repetition is, is a, is a really easy answer. So you just said there, every single morning you'd see me on my stories doing X, Y, and Z. Um, and the biggest thing I've found in my life is that if you want to become a person who is confident, self-assured, respects himself, uh, you need to do the reps which allows that to be true. So that was me putting me severely outside of my comfort zone, doing that on my stories every single day. And it wasn't something that I said consciously in my head thinking, you know, every day for a year I'm gonna do this. It was just more of something that, well, what else am I gonna do? What else am I gonna do?

Am I gonna not do it and just stay inside my comfort zone and not put myself out there? Or do I want to grow and expand and evolve? You know, I think, um, Hormozi or Chris Williamson has has a quote which I'm going to butcher along the lines here of, um, You need to create an underlying stack of proof that you are who you say you are. So if you want to be someone who is confident, you need to create that proof. So throughout my years, like you've touched on, when I was bullied, when I was unconfident, when I grew up with acne, uh, all these different things, I wasn't confident. I had confidence through alcohol.

Confidence was only in my life when I had- um, and it was around that time, COVID, when I was doing the camera stuff, that I stopped drinking as well. I became ill, I'd stopped drinking, um, and I needed to find out who Josh was. And because deep down Josh wasn't confident, you know, on the face of it, to friends and stuff, Yes, Josh was confident, but, you know, deep down on a day-to-day basis, he's not confident putting on this bravado. So in order for me to evolve and expand and become this new version of Josh, to to a point which I am now, where, you know, I'd gladly uh go down to Dubai Marina and just grab my phone and just start talking to the camera, right? I've got I've I've caused

Callum: yeah, Josh: but I can get to that point because I've done the reps. So yeah, that's, that would be literally my, my answer is if there's something that you want to get better at, whatever it is in your life, you need to do it and just expose you to it more, more and more and more. Callum: You're Josh: gonna be terrible at it and that's fine because nobody's watching anyway. And that was the thing, right, that really made me Um, just continue doing what I was doing. And people, sometimes people ask me, what do I need to- I'm, I'm like, yeah, Callum: yeah, yeah, Josh: bro, nobody's watching you anyway. Callum: I think Josh: actually

Callum: I, I still go through these motions now, and correct me if I'm wrong, it's not like you reach that level and that's it, you're done. It's an everyday process of that slipping slide of everything that you have a bad day, it can affect how you project yourself onto other people. So if you have a confidence knock, if you look in the mirror one day and you don't like what you see, that can affect your entire day. But it's like you say, you gotta go out there and just do it. You got- because failing is part of the process. And I think a lot of people miss out on this point that, you know, every successful person, every successful business owner, everyone who has achieved a massive transformation with that body, mind, business, whatever, has had some sort of failure or a string of failures to lead to that point.

They're all lessons you should be learning, Josh: right? Without a doubt. You know, you look at two of the arguably the greatest sports performers in the world, Michael Jordan and Roger Federer. Um, they've they've Callum: more Josh: than they've won, you know. Jordan's lost more points than he's gained. Federer's lost more shots than he's won, you know. Um, and but we think of these people, Callum: oh, Josh: think that, you know, they don't go through shit, you know, you don't- they don't fail. And, you know, they've got to this point and everything's just been like sunshine and rainbows. But, um, it's not true, you know.

I think, like you mentioned, failures- fails are part of life, but it's how you frame it, right? How I You know, you should see failure as an opportunity to educate yourself and grow rather than seeing failure as something that's a bad thing. Because failure means most likely that you've stepped outside of that comfort zone and that you have embraced something different from your self. And you've tried, you've give something a try. Better than not trying at all. Callum: Yeah. Josh: Not trying at all is failure. That's the truth. Trying and not doing something, not working, that, that's just experimentation, you know, that's just Callum: growing.

In my opinion, was a perfect storm for people, um, because you had two people in those camps. You had people who realised that they didn't have enough, so Me personally, I was working a job that I didn't love, but I had everything on the outside. I had all the outside distractions. So, you know, you could go out with friends, you go to the cinema, you go drinking, you can go on holiday. But that's all I've stripped away, and I was one of the unfortunate ones that were. And once you only got that and only think about that, it puts it in perspective for you. And it- I think it pushed people two ways.

Either people got really comfortable with the lifestyle, not having to do anything, and they got really comfortable at home. And then I'm sure you probably had the same thing where you had to put your foot down. It's like, I need to change and I need to grow and I need to try something. So do you think it were a perfect storm when you started doing those things because it gave you a chance to really hone in on running at it as an aspect of building a business, or was it something you've been planning for a while, it was just the time?

Josh: Yeah, so the, the day that, um, I landed back into the UK, Manchester, I remember it very, very strongly, was the day that the next day the country went into lockdown. So I'd been on holiday with two friends to Thailand. We'd been there for 3 weeks, had an amazing time. You wouldn't even know that COVID were a thing in Thailand, right? Like, nobody was talking about it. We were fine. Landed in Manchester, next thing we're all wearing masks and we're like, what on earth is going on? Next thing I look at my emails and my, uh, so I was studying architecture, well, I wasn't studying architecture, I was an architect at the time.

Um, so yeah, as a side tangent, I've got a first class degree in architecture. I was chartered, doing very well in the field as well, but just massively unfulfilled with what I was doing there and Hate is a strong word, but I did, I did hate it. Um, anyway, landed back, max around, look at my emails, the director of my tech firm's like, right, tomorrow morning, because you're back from holiday now, we're gonna get somebody to come and drop off your desk. Callum: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. Josh: So I'm like, amazing. So like, right, okay. But whilst we're on holiday.

With my friends, I was telling them about how much I was hating my job and how much, uh, I'd love to go into the health and fitness space and, you know, do these bits and bobs. And I'd been doing things already prior to that, like secretly in the background of getting my PT calls, doing a little bit here or there, just like on, on, you know, in my free time when I could, just doing, just doing bits. So they were already that, like movement happening for me. But do you know sometimes where you ask somebody a question and you already know what you are going to do or what have you, but sometimes you just want them to confirm before you put your foot down and do it?

It was kind of like one of those things with my friends where it was just a case of, I think I'm gonna do X, Y, and Z. And they were like, Callum: yeah, yeah, Josh: yeah, why haven't you done it already? How? Hal, legend, if you're watching this, my first ever client, best friend, um, at the time. He now lives in Perth in Australia. He was like, I'll be your first client. Okay, great, let's go. So, uh, COVID were an ideal storm for me because I were able to make that transition from architecture to, um, helping people with their health and fitness. Because I was very efficient with what I could do with my architecture.

So don't tell anybody, but I'd get all my architecture work done and then start building the coaching during the workday as well. But during that time period of COVID yeah, I just put my foot on the floor. I just put my foot on the floor, did did everything that I needed to do from an architecture standpoint so nobody would be on my case. But I'd built up such a good reputation that nobody would be on my case anyway in architecture. But worked hard, got all that off. COVID then, um, yeah, so COVID just gave me the opportunity to put my foot down and build this and start growing social media. When COVID finished, I were then doing full-time back in the office, full-time coaching.

And because I were getting some decent results with some rugby friends and coaching some people for, you know, very, very low investment on the side, things were building up really nicely. So yeah, COVID for me was the catalyst of me to be like, right, you've got this time now, Josh. Are you gonna use it or are you gonna lose it? You know, you've got this window of opportunity where nobody's watching over your back if you do a little bit of coaching whilst you should be doing architecture, you know. Um, so yeah, I just took the opportunity with both hands and just put my foot down and, uh, you know, we're here Callum: now. Josh: So Callum: yeah, Josh: and some something Callum: like that.

Looking at it now, it obviously was the right decision. Um, in terms of happiness level and business level and achievement level, it's worked out really well. But you also had architecture. It's a golden ticket for some people. Like, it it can be a very um it's a very high standard qualification, degree. It's something that can take you a lot of places, earn you a lot of money. So why would Josh Lancaster walk away from that type of future that was- it could be pretty set in stone if you get with the right company. You get a decent pension, you get great hours, you get to travel still. Why did you choose coaching?

Josh: So embracing the health and fitness lifestyle was something that really allowed me as a younger As a younger boy to start this first evolution of being somebody who was overweight, unconfident, covered in acne, to somebody who went to the gym for the first time and finally found a position or a doing something where Callum: they Josh: didn't feel any concern about anything. I just did this, I just did the exercise, I just did the reps, I just put the steps in. I'll come out the other side feeling great. And it was that start of my journey, which I remember so vividly, that I wanted other people to experience how good it could feel as well, to change their life through health and fitness.

And because I were able to change my life from a health standpoint, going through what I'd been through, yeah, it was just something that I knew I could help people feel that same, the same level of, of joy and, and confidence and freedom. You know, 'cause when you're bullied, when you're- yeah, when, when you're bullied, when you don't like the look of yourself, when you look at yourself in the mirror or avoid the mirror, that's not how a man should operate. And I, for a lot of my younger life, as soon as I started stepping into the gym and looking after my nutrition more You know what happened? I lost weight. You know what happened? Uh, acne kind of like dampened down at the same time.

You know what happened? Didn't get bullied. Um, so that's the start of me becoming a more confident version of myself. Started playing rugby, you know, I had some amazing times playing rugby. So yeah, the the answer to your question is I found a way of health and fitness completely helping me transform my life, and I wanted to help other people do the same. Second to that, um, I looked at the people in front of me in the architecture firm where I was working and the other two practices that I've worked at before. Stressed. Overweight, grey hair, grey hair at an age of like late 30s, working all hours of God's sense. Um, and that was the direction where I was heading, you know.

I was offered an associate's role before I handed in my notice. I didn't want that for my life, you know. And, um, Seeing that in them, seeing them and looking at myself in the mirror and thinking, this is the direction where I'm heading if things don't change, uh, was Callum: a- And, uh, put me Josh: if Callum: I'm wrong, I've got in my head that you were a Normie boy. Were you Normie or was it Leeds? Josh: Yeah, uh, Leeds. I played for all of Callum: them. This is the thing that Josh: I Callum: always get, because The problem is you can take real stock of what you've got around you, and this isn't a dig at anyone from smaller towns, anything like that.

But the job that you're at, you did the right thing. You look forward and say, that's where I could be. And there's a difference to being comfortable and content. There's like this really fine line, and you can obviously dip into both quite easily. And the way you can flow between both A lot of our conversations we have with potential learners is, I'm earning this money right now. What's the point in starting something new, start from the bottom? It's like, well, it's exciting. You know, have you ever been in a brand new relationship? Have you ever been- drove that car for the first time? Like, the first experience, it's exciting because you have no idea what you're getting into.

And the beautiful thing is we now have a tapestry of people's journeys online, including yours. of these people that have started these journeys. I think fear can take hold of a lot of people to the point where we put ourselves in a bit of a prison. Um, and you walked away from something that is quite profoundly- it could have been a very beneficial career, even though you saw the the later side of it, and you decided to take that jump. So I guess my question is, and I know we've touched on the bullying a little bit, If you didn't have that bullying experience, do you think that you'd be where you are right now? Josh: No, uh, everything happens for a reason. Everything happens for a reason.

That's my, that's my mindset towards everything in life. You know, things, uh, things work out. Great, things don't work out, you know, what's, what's the lessons that we can learn? What's the, what's the next step? What's the growth potential associated with this setback or this challenge or this failure? Um, so yeah, I think everything in life happens for a reason, and I, I firmly do not believe I'd be sitting here right now if I- Callum: yeah, Josh: it's Callum: not like we're advocating it, but I, I were exposed to it myself, so I, I know what you're talking about. It may- it makes you not tough enough, I think that's the wrong word.

It gives you a sense of perspective of when you start bettering yourself and you start seeing, reading between the lines, that usually you get picked out because you're a little bit different. And usually it's an insecurity thing, and that can lead into a superpower, because as you get older Not much can really hurt you. You can really- you understand that type of pain from very young, and you've turned it into a positive. Like I said, um, I mean it as well. You, you're a leader. And this is why I follow these coaches, why I want to talk to people like yourself, because I think with the fitness industry the way it is now, we have more and more people getting certified every day, but not a lot of education towards what the hell you're gonna do with it.

Like, we spoke to people who's been sat on a qualification for years, and their biggest worry is exposing themselves to the world and the world rejecting them. But if anything, like you said, you're performing to nobody for at least, at least the first year. And when we started the podcast, I remember having Josh: a Callum: very distinct conversation with myself saying, who's gonna want to listen to me talk. Like, you, you have these narratives in your head, right, where you're like, you might have the knowledge and you might have the things to bring out there, but you're worried people are going to reject you.

But no one cares up until you get to a certain point, and the negative stuff that you're gonna get is usually just a passing, passing note. So You're sober. Um, that was a bit of a statement, but yeah, yeah, yeah. Josh: No, I just- I'm not in my- didn't just- Callum: So when you met that decision as well, it happened all around Josh: in there. Callum: Do you think that was also better for you in terms of having a clear head and a clear runway? Because I think we grew up in a generation where Well, I think we were sort of the last generation of young men and women going out, the Geordie Shore lifestyle, going out all hours, coming home with a greasy kebab.

Because I find not many people are drinking anymore, and it's definitely a benefit. Josh: Yeah. Callum: Do you think that helps people start taking stock of what they're doing? Um, it definitely helped you, but do you think that's the first step as well? Do you try and help your clients achieve the same thing? Is that part of your package? Do you- is that something that you push? Josh: No, mate, it's not. It's not, to be honest. If I if I somebody comes on board and I know that they are drinking excessively and it's a uh uh you know a weekly occurrence or more, no, I'm I'm open to having that conversation with them.

Just saying, look, you've come here to want you want to achieve X, Y, and Z, but your actions are A, B, and C. You know, it's like, what you want to what you say you want to be, and the person that you say you want Callum: to Josh: be isn't congruent with the actions taken. It's really funny, one of my clients is, uh, I won't- I know I won't name him, but we- I had a similar conversation with him over the past couple of days. He went out over the weekend just passed, um, and, you know, got absolutely hammered. He's like 23-year-old, and, you know, he got- he got drunk and Um, he were really beating himself up about it.

And this might go totally like, Josh, you said this to your client, or like, bro, what you like, why are you beating yourself Callum: up about Josh: it? Like, you're 23. If you've gone out with your friends and just had a really good Callum: time, Josh: like, it's okay. Like, that's fine. You know, like, if if it were twice per week, if it were every week. If it were every other week, then, then I might say something to you and the, the response here might be a little bit different. But I think we've all gotta go on our own path, on our own journey to understand what balance is for us.

And yeah, having a coach or having someone in your corner to tell you if you're going wrong, the wrong way too fast, or, you know, what have you, is important. You know, my client's got really big goals, some really ambitious goals. He wants to be an actor. Um, he's done acting jobs in the past, you know, model, uh, clothing brand, all these things. But is realistically going out and getting hammered once per month against- Callum: no, Josh: that narrative? No, I don't think so, you know. So do I- I, I don't think becoming sober is Was it for me? 100%. I I would not be sitting here right now if I was still drinking the way I was. But I was drinking super heavy.

Every Saturday, you know, there would be culture, mate. No, every Saturday I would get blackout, but I would get blackout drunk. Every just black blackout drunk. And I mean, to a point where I would not remember getting up. I wouldn't- sorry, I would not remember getting home. Um, and it was just too frequent, and, and I had enough, you know. I was going through some other struggles at the time with my health, um, and, you know, alcohol wasn't helping with that. Then, you know, the coaching, all these things building that up wasn't helping because, you know, as heavy as I was drinking, it wasn't- it's not just the day after, it's after the day after the day after the day after, right?

And you just get around, you know. What even is this, you know? So, um, do I think that people can succeed in life, I guess, with having a few drinks every now and again or getting hammered every now and again? Yeah, I think, I think they certainly can. Um, do I think it was a catalyst for me and something that I look back on in terms of where I'm at right now was a Callum: massive- I think it's a guilt as well, right? Um, As obviously social media, it comes up a lot of topics because for everything that you do, there'll be something on social media that makes you feel guilty about it. And that's usually the algorithms working against you in that way.

Uh, it brings it around and it shows you stuff. And you know, I had one the other day. I didn't get home in time to say goodnight to my daughter, and then I saw a video pop up. 20 minutes later, say I should say good night to your daughter every night, and then you start feeling of guilt. I'm just like- but that's what it does. And I think people who see that, and then all they get is people getting sober videos or people with catastrophic stories where, you know- and I think that's where it's relevant. And then even with business, right, like you're having a rough time building your business, and then you're seeing videos of people who Sometimes it helps when they're going through their struggles, or you're getting people like, um, I can't remember his name, but he's a famous salesman, and he's like, you just need to stop being a bitch.

If your account doesn't have $30,000 in it, then what are you doing? Like, problem is the messaging that we get over social media influences the world in such a way where it can either stop them or push them forward or push them in the wrong direction, right? And I think, uh, it's, it's relevant to have those conversations, but also you've gotta realise that social media, for a lot of intents and purposes, is 90% unreal. Like, what you're seeing is very short snippets of very choreographed and very unrealistic expectations. And I guess I'm bringing this round Um, to my main question is Dubai.

So, online coach living in Dubai, this is what I'd call a stereotype in terms of the way it's projected online. But what made you go in that direction? Because you're actually doing the thing and you're actually doing what you say you're doing, and you've got a reason to be out there. So why did you choose it? What was the reason for being there? I know you've travelled quite a lot. Josh: So for the past 3 years or so, I've been on almost like a, a nomadic journey where, um, I spend anywhere from 90 days to 6 months in different countries. Just, just to be fair, mate, just like finding myself again. So I've gone through this period where I was really, really ill, lost loads of weight.

Um, I stopped drinking, stopped playing rugby, saw my bicep playing rugby, and played a game since. Um, and lost a lot of friends during that process. So I found myself in the UK with a very, very, very- like, could count them on that, those four fingers- friends in the, in the UK. Um, and but my own, my own fault. didn't socialise when I stopped drinking, you know, secluded myself, um, through the illness and things that I were experiencing as well. So I found myself just kind of like being isolated in my own hometown through the fault of my own. Um, so I just thought, you know what, I've always wanted to travel, I'm gonna do some travelling.

I've got a business now where I can literally pick up laptop and go do what I want. So that was So I've travelled, travelled around the world looking at different places and essentially wanting to find a new home. That, that was the idea, uh, want to find a place Callum: where Josh: I felt good, where I felt at home, where I felt like I'd be able to build a, a great, uh, community around me where I'd have great friends and great connections. have a- find an amazing partner, you know, and settle down and have a life here. And there were various different places which fit that bill. Um, some of them didn't work out for various reasons, visa issues mainly.

Um, but again, everything happens for a reason. Uh, if my visa had worked out for Spain, for example, I wouldn't be sitting here right now, but it didn't. So, you know, everything happens for a reason, and I made the decision, uh, reached out to a good, a good group of close personal friends of mine who, who live here and who have lived here for, you know, a very long time. Um, and during that period of me travelling, I come here for a period of time as well. And, you know, I've always said about the place, extremely safe, extremely clean. Um, I don't have a bad word to say about it. So I thought, why not? Let's just give it a go. Let's just, let's just go.

Um, and honestly, the first 3 weeks I've been here, literally just moved over, so super, super fresh. I feel the most alive and energetic. Callum: Does, uh, Josh now, who's achieved this, who's still on the journey, would Josh 8 years ago believe that? Josh: No, no, no. Josh, 8 years- Josh, Josh now still has self-doubt and still fears things and still has those insecurities and that anxiety. Um, funny, this morning I've just invested in a coach Callum: that Josh: can help me with those type of things- fear, anxiety. mindset coach, you could call him, or a, yeah, performance coach, something like that.

Um, because yeah, like, I don't have all my shit together, but I'm a lot better now than where I was, you know, 3 weeks, 6 months ago, 12 months ago. Um, so no, would, would Josh 8 years ago think I'd be sitting here right now having this conversation on this podcast? No. I think, um, Yeah, it's a laugh. And, uh, definitely- Callum: That's a nice thing to think though, right? Josh: Like, Callum: it's a nice thing to think that you proved yourself wrong so many times. Like, it's such a nice standard to have where, you know, you could say that 8 years ago, there's no way we're gonna do that, and then you can just keep proving yourself wrong. You have an achievement.

I mean, I suppose my biggest question is, what does it take to do this, because I could answer this question for learners out there, people who are curious. I could answer it many different ways, but sometimes not just coming from me helps, and not just coming from other coaches. Like, I like to get a nest egg of different people's opinions, and it's like, here, there's 20 different opinions on what it takes to make something of this. And specifically towards coaching, what do you think it takes in like the minerals of somebody to be able to make a go of this and some kind of success?

Josh: Yeah, um, I think we're in a culture at the moment in time where people have drifted to a position where They don't care enough. And it's cool to care. It's cool to care about something and be passionate about something and have energy around something and give positive vibes to doing something. It's cool to care about client success. Callum: It's Josh: cool to care about business. And despite anything and everything, if you don't care about people who are coming on board and you're just doing something for paycheck at the end of the month, for your own notoriety or whatever it may be, you're doing it for the wrong things, you know. You're doing it for the wrong things.

You need to Care about everybody that is coming into your, coming into your path. Because when you care, you're gonna help them get some amazing results. And you know what the primary thing is above anything else? It's results. It's a results-based business. You know, every client that comes into my door, come in here to get a result. I tell them that all the time. You know, you're here to get a result. And I'm gonna partner alongside of you. I'm gonna help you make sure that it happens. I'm gonna hold you accountable and give you a slap around the back of the ears if I need to, but also at the same time, I give you a pat on the back and tell you well done.

You know, and caring about people who are in your circle and who are in your programme and doing everything in your power to help them achieve the results that they've come for. Callum: Why did them- Why do people trust you? What did you do to build that trust for people to come forward to you? Josh: Yeah, I think it's a great question. I think I've just, Callum: uh, Josh: I show vulnerability. I'd like to think I'm very authentic and true to myself online, and I show my vulnerability. Um, we're in an age where People buy into people, right? So if you're not putting yourself out there, if you're not showing who you are as a real person and you're just this man behind a, a bicep curl tutorial video, or this is how you do a lat pulldown, this is how you're gonna get 5 more pull-ups, nobody cares, bro.

Nobody cares anymore. Yeah, 5 years ago that might have been okay, but I don't know if, like, I don't, I don't, I don't know if you, you've, uh, you're in the 21st century and you can get uh any programme. Callum: Well, the Scott Herman era is over, innit? Josh: ChatGPT. Callum: Do you remember Scott Herman? Yeah. It doesn't work like that anymore. Josh: Don't- yeah, like, nobody cares because all that information's Callum: just Josh: so readily available to you. It's online, it's on AI, it is what it is. If you wanna, if you wanna grow and you want people to trust you, you need to document yourself. You need to show your own personal standards.

Callum: Well, if the only issue- the only barrier was information, Josh: right, Callum: we'd be out of a job because we've got We've got an AI, we've got Google, we've got thousands of videos on YouTube showing every exercise you could possibly think of, every nutrition programme. You know, you could go on ChatGPT now, put in all your stats, it'll give you a perfect programme on a perfect nutrition plan. If the problem was just getting the information, it wouldn't- we wouldn't be needed. I mean, you gotta think about the people who have that programme in front of them and don't do anything with it. Is it because they just don't want to do it? Is it because they don't know how?

Is it because they need someone there to give them a simpler step? Are they over-egging themselves? Are they- like, all these things. This is the thing that gets me all the time. faqs.a: Josh Lancaster is an online coach who was a chartered architect with a first-class degree before he left the profession, massively unfulfilled, to coach people full time. He built his coaching business on the side of his architecture job during COVID and now lives and works in Dubai. You can find him on Instagram and YouTube as @joshlancasterj2.

faqs.q: How did Josh get his first coaching client?
faqs.a: He flew home from three weeks in Thailand the day before the UK went into lockdown and told his friends what he wanted to do. His best friend at the time said he would be his first client. Josh says COVID was an ideal storm for him, because it let him make the move from architecture to coaching.

faqs.q: What question does Josh ask before paying for a mentor or coach?
faqs.a: "Would I want their life?" He says it is the number one question he asks before investing in anybody. Great transformations and a big following count for little if you aren't inspired by how that person lives; a coach who drives a Lamborghini is no use to you if a Lamborghini means nothing to you.

faqs.q: How did Josh build confidence on camera?
faqs.a: Repetition. Josh says the reps are what allow you to become a confident, self-assured person, which is why he showed up on his Instagram stories every morning on the way to work or the gym. He also stopped drinking around the same time, after years of getting blackout drunk every Saturday, and says he would not be where he is now if he hadn't.

faqs.q: Why does Josh say clients don't care about exercise tutorials any more?
faqs.a: Because people buy into people. Anyone can get a training plan in seconds, so a coach who hides behind bicep curl and lat pull-down videos gives clients no reason to choose them. Josh shows who he is, including his vulnerability, and says that is what builds trust.

faqs.q: Is training two sessions a week enough?
faqs.a: Josh's view is that training does not have to be five or six days a week forever. Two sessions a week that a client can keep up forever is more sustainable than a 12-week plan, after which many people put the weight back on or fall into on-and-off cycles.

faqs.q: What values should a new personal trainer bring to the job?
faqs.a: Josh's answer is care and passion: care about your clients enough to understand their pains, problems and struggles, and work from a place of joy and play rather than fear and anxiety. He says many trainers are scared to show passion because of judgement, but that energy is what is infectious.
